```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, comment = "##", fig.align = "center")
library(NNS)
library(quantmod)
# Yahoo Finance data for the financial sections, when it can be downloaded.
yahoo <- function(sym, ...) tryCatch(getSymbols(sym, src = "yahoo", auto.assign = FALSE, ...),
                                     error = function(e) NULL)
fred <- function(id) {
  d <- tryCatch(read.csv(paste0("https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=", id),
                         na.strings = "."), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(d)) return(NULL)
  xts::xts(as.numeric(d[[2]]), as.Date(d[[1]]), dimnames = list(NULL, id))
}
# Download everything once; a section runs only when all of its series arrived.
fin <- lapply(c(SPY = "SPY", GLD = "GLD", TLT = "TLT", FXE = "FXE"), yahoo)
fin_ok <- !any(vapply(fin, is.null, logical(1)))
spy_long <- if (fin_ok) yahoo("SPY", from = "1965-01-01")
mzm <- fred("MZMNS")
dgs10 <- fred("DGS10")
mag_ok <- fin_ok && !is.null(spy_long) && !is.null(mzm) && !is.null(dgs10)
```

# Install NNS

We need the latest version of NNS available on GitHub.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
require(devtools); install_github('OVVO-Financial/NNS', ref = "NNS-Beta-Version")
require(NNS)
```

# Nonlinear Scaling Normalization

NNS nonlinear scaling normalization involves using the degree of nonlinearity
between variables to then transform the values to a shared range.

NNS's technique is different than linear scaling where all variables are
assumed to have a perfect linear relationship (and by extension wind up with
the same mean); and different than standardization
($\frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$) which does not consider variable relationships.

NNS is also different than quantile normalization, which as we'll show is not
robust to different original scale values in multivariate problems.

# Examples

A multivariate example of each technique will highlight the differences.

We will use the quintessential quantile normalization example on Wikipedia as
well as a more intricate financial variable example.

```{r data, fig.height = 4}
A <- c(5, 4, 3); B <- c(2, 1, 4); C <- c(3, 4, 6); D <- c(4, 2, 8)
matplot(cbind(A, B, C, D), type = 'l')
```

## Linear Scaling

NNS offers a linear scaling option which essentially sets the correlation
between variables to 1.

```{r linear, fig.height = 4}
lin.norm.variables <- NNS.norm(cbind(A, B, C, D), chart.type = 'l', linear = TRUE)
```

A quick check verifies all of the means are equal for the linear scaling
technique:

```{r linear-check}
t(lin.norm.variables)

apply(lin.norm.variables, 2, function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)))
```

## Standard Standardization

Variables after going through a standard standardization technique will have a
zero mean and unit variance. The following demonstrates the results.

```{r standard, fig.height = 4}
matplot(scale(cbind(A, B, C, D)), type = 'l')
```

Means = 0; variances = 1...

```{r standard-check}
apply(scale(cbind(A, B, C, D)), 2, function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)))
```

## NNS Nonlinear Scaling

We can now compare the nonlinear scaling normalization technique.

```{r nonlinear, fig.height = 4}
nonlin.norm.variables <- NNS.norm(cbind(A, B, C, D), chart.type = 'l')
```

And we note the difference in means along with the smaller standard deviation
for each transformed variable versus the other methods.

```{r nonlinear-check}
t(nonlin.norm.variables)

apply(nonlin.norm.variables, 2, function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)))
```

## Quantile Normalization

Quantile normalization is a technique for making two or more distributions
identical in statistical properties. This is the antithesis of `NNS.norm` as
we seek to retain the uniqueness of each distribution while creating a shared
range of observations.

The PDF used `normalize.quantiles()` from Bioconductor's **preprocessCore**
(`BiocManager::install("preprocessCore")`). When it is not installed, the
base R version below averages the sorted columns and gives tied values their
lowest rank, as in the Wikipedia example.

```{r quantile-function}
if (requireNamespace("preprocessCore", quietly = TRUE)) {
  normalize.quantiles <- preprocessCore::normalize.quantiles
} else {
  normalize.quantiles <- function(x) {
    means <- rowMeans(apply(x, 2, sort))
    apply(x, 2, function(z) means[rank(z, ties.method = "min")])
  }
}
```

```{r quantile}
# QN function expects a matrix...create a matrix using the same example
mat <- matrix(c(5, 2, 3, 4, 4, 1, 4, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8),
              ncol = 3)
row.names(mat) <- c("A", "B", "C", "D")
mat

qn.mat <- apply(normalize.quantiles(mat), 1, function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)))
colnames(qn.mat) <- c("A", "B", "C", "D")

QN <- normalize.quantiles(mat)
```

Comparing all methods with the original dataset yields:

```{r compare-small, fig.height = 3.5}
# Rotate matrix for plotting as QN is row based variables
QN <- t(QN[1:nrow(QN), ])

# Plot
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
matplot(QN, type = 'l')
title(main = "Quantile Normalization")
matplot(nonlin.norm.variables, type = 'l')
title(main = "Nonlinear Normalization")
matplot(lin.norm.variables, type = 'l')
title(main = "Linear Normalization")
```

# Financial Series Example

Let's load some financial variables that have overlapping prices...

```{r financial-data, eval = fin_ok, fig.height = 4}
# fin: daily prices downloaded from Yahoo Finance in the setup chunk
SPY <- Cl(to.monthly(fin$SPY))
GLD <- Cl(to.monthly(fin$GLD))
TLT <- Cl(to.monthly(fin$TLT))
FXE <- Cl(to.monthly(fin$FXE))
A <- as.matrix(cbind(SPY, GLD, TLT, FXE))
A <- A[complete.cases(A), ]

# Plot
matplot(A, type = 'l')
legend('topleft', legend = c("SPY", "GLD", "TLT", "FXE"), col = seq_len(ncol(A)),
       fill = seq_len(ncol(A)), horiz = TRUE, bty = 'n')
```

Comparing all methods with the original dataset yields:

```{r financial-compare, eval = fin_ok, fig.height = 3.5}
# Rotate matrix to variables by row for QN
qn.mat <- t(A[1:nrow(A), ])
QN <- normalize.quantiles(qn.mat)
nonlin.norm.variables <- NNS.norm(A)
lin.norm.variables <- NNS.norm(A, linear = TRUE)

# Rotate QN results so matplot can use columns
QN <- t(QN[1:nrow(QN), ])

# Plot
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
matplot(QN, type = 'l')
title(main = "Quantile Normalization")
matplot(nonlin.norm.variables, type = 'l')
title(main = "Nonlinear Normalization")
matplot(lin.norm.variables, type = 'l')
title(main = "Linear Normalization")
```

```{r financial-skipped, echo = FALSE, eval = !fin_ok, results = "asis"}
cat("*Yahoo Finance data could not be downloaded when this document was built, so this section was not run.*")
```

Note the tighter overall range for `NNS.norm`.

# Non-overlapping variables

When the variables do not share any ranges of observations, quantile
normalization merely reports the mean value for that variable.

```{r nonoverlap-data, fig.height = 4}
set.seed(123)
x <- rnorm(100); y = rnorm(100) + 5; z = rnorm(100) + 10
A <- as.matrix(cbind(x, y, z))
nonlin.norm.variables <- NNS.norm(A)
lin.norm.variables <- NNS.norm(A, linear = TRUE)

# Plot
matplot(A, type = 'l')
legend('topleft', legend = colnames(A), col = seq_len(ncol(A)),
       fill = seq_len(ncol(A)), horiz = TRUE, bty = 'n')

# Rotate matrix to variables by row for QN
qn.mat <- t(A[1:nrow(A), ])
QN <- normalize.quantiles(qn.mat)
```

Quantiles have a problem...

```{r nonoverlap-compare, fig.height = 3.5}
# Rotate QN results so matplot can use columns
QN <- t(QN[1:nrow(QN), ])

# Plot
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
matplot(QN, type = 'l')
title(main = "Quantile Normalization")
matplot(nonlin.norm.variables, type = 'l')
title(main = "Nonlinear Normalization")
matplot(lin.norm.variables, type = 'l')
title(main = "Linear Normalization")
```

# Orders of Magnitude Reduced

We can successfully remove orders of magnitude differences between variables.
Here is a financial example using money supply (MZM) measured in billions of
dollars, the S&P 500 (SPY) closing prices measured in points and US 10-year
Treasury yields (Ts) measured in percentage points.

```{r magnitude, eval = mag_ok, fig.height = 4}
# spy_long from Yahoo Finance; mzm and dgs10 from FRED (setup chunk)
SPY <- Ad(to.monthly(spy_long['1962::']))
MZM <- mzm['1962::']
Ts <- Cl(to.monthly(dgs10['1962::']))
A <- as.matrix(merge(SPY, MZM, Ts, join = "inner"))
A <- A[complete.cases(A), ]

# Plot
matplot(A, type = 'l')
legend('topleft', legend = c("SPY", "MZM", "Ts"), col = seq_len(ncol(A)),
       fill = seq_len(ncol(A)), horiz = TRUE, bty = 'n')
```

```{r magnitude-compare, eval = mag_ok, fig.height = 3.5}
# Rotate matrix to variables by row for QN
qn.mat <- t(A[1:nrow(A), ])
nonlin.norm.variables <- NNS.norm(A)
lin.norm.variables <- NNS.norm(A, linear = TRUE)
QN <- normalize.quantiles(qn.mat)

# Rotate QN results so matplot can use columns
QN <- t(QN[1:nrow(QN), ])

# Plot
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
matplot(QN, type = 'l')
title(main = "Quantile Normalization")
matplot(nonlin.norm.variables, type = 'l')
title(main = "Nonlinear Normalization")
matplot(lin.norm.variables, type = 'l')
title(main = "Linear Normalization")
```

```{r magnitude-skipped, echo = FALSE, eval = !mag_ok, results = "asis"}
cat("*Yahoo Finance or FRED data could not be downloaded when this document was built, so this section was not run.*")
```

> **Note (2026).** `NNS.norm` multiplies each column by a scaling factor.
> Positive factors preserve Pearson correlations; a negative factor reverses
> the sign of that column's correlations. Check the factors' signs before
> interpreting associations between normalized variables (see
> `examples/example-corrections.md`).

# Practical Applications

Normalization eliminates the need for multiple y-axis charts and prohibits the
misuse thereof. Furthermore, placing variables on the same axes with shared
ranges permits a more relevant conditional probability analysis, which along
with time normalization is used in the `NNS.caus()` routine for identifying
causal relationships between variables.

To learn more about NNS statistics and their theoretical foundations, see
*Nonlinear Nonparametric Statistics: Using Partial Moments*
(<https://ovvo-financial.github.io/NNS/book/>). More NNS examples are posted
on GitHub: <https://github.com/OVVO-Financial/NNS/blob/NNS-Beta-Version/examples/index.md>
